## About this course

**Claude Code for Accounting Research: AI Agents for the Empirical Researcher** is a five-module, hands-on intensive plus a closing half-day seminar, built for accounting PhD students and faculty with mixed Stata/Python backgrounds and no assumed experience with agentic AI tools. It teaches Claude Code as a research assistant that lives in the terminal — one that reads and writes files, runs your existing code, and iterates — and it spends as much time on verification as on capability, because faster output is worthless if you can't trust it. The five build modules cover: foundations and the tool ladder, an empirical loop on free SEC data, EDGAR text as a measured panel plus a first Skill, WRDS at scale through an MCP server with a Stata bridge, and writing/safety/verification as a capstone. A closing seminar asks what an agent this capable changes about how accounting research gets produced, and which parts of the job stay with the researcher.

## Attribution

**Original authorship.** The notes, labs, slides, and figures on this site are original teaching material written for this course. Where this course draws on an external idea, technique, or example, it is cited in the text or listed on the [Resources](resources.qmd) page rather than reproduced.

**Goldsmith-Pinkham / Markus Academy series.** Several of this course's teaching examples and prompt patterns were inspired by Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham's "Claude Code for Economists" series for the Markus Academy (Ep. 162).

**Barrios Skills collection.** The [Skills catalog](skills/index.qmd) is a snapshot of the Barrios Skills collection, included under its MIT license (reproduced in full at `skills/LICENSE.txt` and linked from the catalog index). The live collection at [barrios88.github.io/barrios-skills](https://barrios88.github.io/barrios-skills/) remains the canonical, actively updated source; this site's copy is a point-in-time snapshot taken when the course was built.

**Figure and exhibit policy.** Figures on this site (the tool ladder, the empirical loop, the verification-debt 2×2, and the rest) are original diagrams drawn for this course. A small number of exhibits show what a Claude Code or Claude Desktop session looks like in practice — for example, the Module 1 terminal-anatomy and permission-prompt exhibits. These are mock-ups of a typical interaction, not screenshots or transcripts of any single real session; each is labeled as such in its caption.

**External links.** The links on the [Resources](resources.qmd) page point to real, existing projects — including the one item flagged as unvetted rather than recommended.

**No Yale trademarks.** This is a personal course site by a Yale faculty member, not an official Yale or Yale School of Management site.
